title: Arrow prayers (Nehemiah 2:4)
hookLine: before the king answers, Nehemiah fires a silent prayer upward

cards: Someone important turns to you and says: so, what do you want? The interview. The doctor.
The boss with one minute between meetings. Your mouth is open, and there's no time to think. The same question once came in the Persian court, about four and a half centuries before Jesus.
A Jewish man named Nehemiah is cupbearer to King Artaxerxes: he serves the king's wine. He's just heard that the walls of Jerusalem are rubble, and he can't hide his grief.
The king notices his sad face, and the text says, "Then I was very sore afraid." A sad servant in front of a king was a risk. Then the king asks the question.

teach.h: A PRAYER BETWEEN QUESTION AND ANSWER.
teach.b: Here's the verse, in the King James Bible: "Then the king said unto me, For what dost thou make request? So I prayed to the God of heaven." And in the very next breath, he answers the king.
No words recorded, no kneeling, no closed eyes. Between the question and the answer, a prayer went up, and nobody in the room saw it.
Christians came to call this an arrow prayer: short, silent, fired upward in the middle of life.
Augustine wrote of monks in the Egyptian desert, the same desert as the Jesus Prayer, who prayed all day in quick, brief bursts. But the arrow didn't come from nowhere.
In chapter one, when the bad news first came, Nehemiah sat down and wept, and fasted and prayed for days.

teach.h: THE BOW WAS STRUNG FOR MONTHS.
teach.b: Months passed before the king ever asked. So the arrow flew from a bow that had been strung for a long time. The long prayer and the short one belong together.
The Bible is full of these arrows.

teach.h: LORD, HELP ME. LORD, SAVE ME.
teach.b: A mother pleading for her daughter, in Matthew: "Lord, help me." Peter, sinking into the waves: "Lord, save me." Three words each.
Catholics, Orthodox Christians and Protestants all have their short prayers for the middle of things. For Nehemiah, it worked: the king said yes, and he went home to rebuild the wall.

how: Many Christians pray short, silent prayers through the day, before a meeting, at a siren, in a moment of fear, alongside longer times of prayer; Orthodox Christians often use the Jesus Prayer this way.

o: prayers for soldiers going out to battle
quick, silent prayers in the middle of life

games.q: who said it, who did it — tap the pairs.

s: the Bible gives the words of Nehemiah's quick prayer
it only says he prayed to the God of heaven. the words aren't recorded.
Nehemiah had already been praying about this for a long time
in chapter one he wept, fasted and prayed for days. the king's question came months later.
short prayers belong to only one church
Catholics, Orthodox Christians and Protestants all pray short prayers in the middle of the day.

games.q: you're Nehemiah. the king has seen your sad face and asks what you want. you have about one second. what do you do?
o: answer at once with the whole plan.
games.why: "So I prayed to the God of heaven." then he answered. the king said yes, and Nehemiah went home to rebuild Jerusalem's walls.

practice: Think of the next conversation you'll have today, with a coworker, a child, a cashier, someone on the phone, and picture the moment before the first word.

If you pray, send up a short line in three seconds, like the mother's "Lord, help me," or a few words of your own; if you don't, take one slow breath and wish them well. Then let the rest of the time be quiet.

wordCard.voice: Arrow prayers. Short, silent prayers sent up in the middle of life, like Nehemiah's before the king. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: prayer. the verb in Nehemiah 2:4, "I prayed," comes from the same root.

carryVoice: Your line: short prayers fly. Nobody in the room has to know. That's one hundred three.
